paragraphs: One-sentence judgment: a barista is not “someone who can do latte art,” but a store position that prepares and serves specialty coffee and other beverages and plated food according to recipes and procedures: taking orders and relaying them to colleagues, preparing hot or cold beverages according to recipes (coffee and espresso drinks and blended coffee and tea), weighing and grinding and packaging coffee beans, preparing and serving menu items such as sandwiches and salads, wrapping and labeling and dating food for sale, checking freezer and refrigerator and heating equipment temperatures, cleaning and disinfecting work areas and utensils and equipment, taking out trash and cleaning service areas, ordering and restocking and arranging displays, describing the menu to customers and demonstrating equipment use, and collecting and processing payments; it is not suitable for people who only want to produce by feel, are unwilling to verify portions and extraction and temperature and time according to recipes, and are unwilling to treat utensil disinfection and equipment temperature checks and cleaning as part of the job.

Signals to keep exploring: you are willing to verify portions and extraction and temperature and time item by item according to recipes and standard procedures, you can stay accurate and hygienic in the rhythm of peak queues, continuous standing, and repetitive motions, you take the initiative to verify equipment temperatures and food labels and shelf lives, you are willing to confirm first and then handle customer complaints or order anomalies, and you can truthfully record handovers and temperatures and cleaning and exceptions.

Conditions for pausing investment first: you have not yet completed a full order-taking—preparation—serving—cleaning—recording loop under any supervised conditions, or you can only explain your interest by saying “I like drinking coffee”; also do not treat having made coffee at home or having taken a hobby course as proof that you can independently operate commercial equipment or independently bear food safety, equipment shutdown, or refund responsibility. Hot beverage, steam, and equipment burn protection, food allergens and temperature control, food label and shelf life verification, customer information and payment information handling, and food safety and shutdown and refund authority must be carried out in accordance with the applicable jurisdiction and the competent authority and employer systems and must leave traceable records; this page does not provide any recipes, extraction parameters, or equipment operating instructions.

Occupational identity and definition must be verified separately: O*NET lists 35-3023.01 (Baristas) as Job Zone 1–2 (SVP below 6.0); among the educational attainment the page publishes, 64% require less than a high school diploma, 29% require a high school diploma or equivalent, and 2% require a postsecondary certificate; the corresponding chapter of the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook lists the typical entry-level education for this combined group as no formal educational credential, with no related work experience required and short-term on-the-job training. It must also be noted: the wage, employment, and industry data on this page are explicitly labeled on the O*NET page as taken from the same-family parent occupation 35-3023.00 (Fast Food and Counter Workers), and are not a barista-only definition; the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook chapter is also the combined “Food and Beverage Serving and Related Workers” group, which is broader than the same-family parent occupation. Education, training, certification, employer hiring, and in-store task authorization are different statuses and must be verified item by item according to employer and position and jurisdiction.

In one sentence: this is a store service position that delivers steadily by verifying item by item according to recipes and standard procedures and working through the rhythm of peak periods, continuous standing, and repetitive motions, with the core being beverage preparation and serving, equipment temperature checks, utensil disinfection, and records — not an interest in coffee or an imagination about social media; its U.S. wage and employment data must be read under the same-family parent occupation definition.

The work of baristas can be divided into three categories: preparation and serving services (taking orders and relaying them to other colleagues for preparation; preparing or serving hot or cold beverages such as coffee and espresso drinks and blended coffee and tea according to recipes; weighing and grinding and packaging coffee beans; making or serving menu items such as sandwiches or salads; serving prepared foods such as muffins, biscotti, and bagels; describing menu items to customers or recommending products that might appeal to them; providing product details such as coffee blends or brewing methods to customers; demonstrating the use of retail equipment such as espresso machines; slicing fruit and vegetables and desserts or meats as needed); hygiene and safety and records (cleaning or disinfecting work areas and utensils and equipment; cleaning service or seating areas; taking out trash; checking freezer and refrigerator or heating equipment temperatures to ensure proper operation; wrapping and labeling or dating food for sale; restocking paper goods or beverage preparation materials at the customer service counter; making signs labeling store products or events); and customer reception and store operations (collecting and processing customer payments; ordering and receiving and inventory replenishment or retail products; setting up or restocking merchandise displays; providing explanations about products and preparation; responding to customer complaints and special requests within the authorized scope). All three categories presume stopping to verify first when an order is unclear, equipment temperature is abnormal, food contamination is suspected, or the situation exceeds your authorization.

O*NET occupational identity and tasks: O*NET 35-3023.01 Baristas (page updated 2026, Bright Outlook). The official duties are to prepare or serve specialty coffee and other beverages and to serve food such as baked goods and sandwiches to customers; there are 19 official tasks (17 core and 2 supplemental), with core task importance scores from 96 to 71 and supplemental tasks of 46 and 35. The work activities page lists 41 items with importance scores, the highest being identifying objects, actions, and events 61, performing for or working directly with the public 59, communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates 58, getting information 57, resolving conflicts and negotiating with others 54, establishing and maintaining interpersonal relationships 50, training and teaching others 46, handling and moving objects 45, and making decisions and solving problems 45. There are 20 detailed work activities (no scores). The task list describes group work and does not mean every position performs all tasks.

entries: Order taking and confirmation | Give the service a basis | Receive customer orders and repeat them back for confirmation, relay orders to other colleagues for preparation, and explain the feasible scope and waiting time.

Beverage preparation and serving | Give the output a specification | Weigh and grind and extract according to recipes and standard procedures, and prepare and serve hot or cold beverages and menu items.

Food preparation and labeling | Keep risk controlled | Prepare or serve menu items such as sandwiches and salads according to procedure, and wrap and label food for sale and verify shelf lives and first-in-first-out.
Equipment and temperature checks | Make the process reviewable | Check freezer and refrigerator or heating equipment temperatures, confirm proper operation, and handle abnormalities.
Cleaning and disinfection | Make hygiene traceable | Clean or disinfect work areas and utensils and equipment, clean service and seating areas, take out trash, and handle waste.

Cashiering and store operations | Keep the business running | Collect and process customer payments, order and receive and restock and arrange displays, and respond to customer requests and record exceptions within the authorized scope.

Work environment | 94% continuously or almost continuously stand, 67% continuously or almost continuously use hands to handle, control, or feel objects and tools, 47% continuously or almost continuously make repetitive motions (another 32% more than half the time), 36% continuously or almost continuously walk or run, and 23% bend or twist the body about half the time; 100% are in contact with others continuously, 86% have face-to-face discussions every day, 66% work very close (within touching distance) to others, and 29% have telephone conversations every day; 92% work indoors in an environmentally controlled setting every day and 18% work indoors without environmental control every day; 43% are exposed to extreme heat or cold every day, 44% are exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise every day, 26% are exposed to minor burns, cuts, bites, or stings every day, 19% are exposed to contaminants every day, and 17% wear common protective or safety equipment every day; 92% are never in hazardous conditions, 94% never come into contact with hazardous equipment, and 97% are never exposed to disease or infections; 68% never sit, and 79% kneel, crouch, bend, or crawl less than half the time.
Main equipment and tools | Espresso machines and grinders and cold beverage and steam equipment, freezers and refrigerators and heating equipment and thermometers, coffee beans and tea leaves and dairy products and syrups and ingredients and prepared foods, cleaning and disinfection supplies and disposables, cash register and ordering and inventory systems, and personal protection (gloves, aprons, and burn protection as the work requires).
Task rhythm | 88% have a typical workweek of less than 40 hours; 52% have a regular schedule and 40% an irregular schedule; 16% face time pressure every day (64% never); 33% have a lot of freedom in decisions and 39% some freedom; 55% consider the work slightly automated and 22% consider it not at all automated; 22% consider the pace determined by equipment speed very important (25% consider it not at all important).
Collaboration | Collaborate with baristas on the same shift and with back-of-house and front-desk colleagues; 64% consider working with a work group or team extremely important (another 23% very important), 15% bear very high responsibility for the health and safety of others (another 44% moderate responsibility), and 76% consider dealing with external customers or the public extremely important (another 22% very important).
Competition and pressure | 35% consider precision or accuracy extremely important (another 35% very important and 30% important); 23% deal with unpleasant or angry people every day (53% at least once a week); 24% are in conflict situations at least once a week; 20% consider the consequences of error serious; 40% consider competition slight and 27% consider there to be no competition at all.
Compliance and safety | Beverage preparation and serving and utensil disinfection and equipment temperature must meet applicable food safety and venue hygiene and equipment safety requirements; on the U.S. side, the BLS notes that this combined group usually has no formal education or experience requirement and that skills are learned on the job; O*NET lists 3 national certifications (including coffee and food service fields). Article 44 of China's Food Safety Law requires food production and operation enterprises to carry out food safety knowledge training; Article 45 requires personnel engaged in work that comes into contact with directly edible food to undergo an annual health examination and obtain a health certificate before starting work. Specific equipment, refund, and management authority must be verified separately with the employer and cannot be inferred from education or occupational certificates.
Records and retrospective | Orders and output, equipment temperature checks, utensil cleaning and disinfection handling, food label and shelf life verification, and customer feedback and exceptions need to be traceable.
Skills and training | O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone 1–2 (SVP below 6.0); basic skills are led by active listening 60, speaking 56, monitoring 50, reading comprehension 47, and critical thinking 41; transferable skills are led by service orientation 60, coordination 50, social perceptiveness 50, operation and control 41, persuasion 38, negotiation 35, and time management 35; knowledge is led by customer and personal service 89, administration and management 65, sales and marketing 62, food production 54, and English language 52; the current abilities list includes speech clarity, oral comprehension, oral expression, and control precision; work styles are social orientation 73, cooperation 69, dependability 69, attention to detail 55, and self control 50, none of which are individual admission scores.
Entry and authorization | Education and certification do not equal equipment operation or food safety determinations or shutdown and refund authority; the BLS notes that this combined group usually has no formal education or experience requirement and that skills are learned on the job; O*NET lists 3 national certifications, none of which equals a hiring threshold or employer appointment.
Industry and employers | The O*NET industry distribution is accommodation and food services 87% and other industries (including retail trade) 13% (same-family parent occupation definition); common employers are chain brand stores, independent coffee shops, and retail, hotel, and institutional beverage bars.
Preparation and serving services

U.S. wages are under the parent occupation 35-3023.00 definition, not barista-only. For 2025 OEWS, annual salary percentiles 10 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 90 are 22,840 / 27,700 / 31,200 / 36,070 / 42,650 USD; hourly wages are 10.98 / 13.32 / 15.00 / 17.34 / 20.51 USD. This covers full-time and part-time wage-and-salary workers, includes tips, commissions, and production bonuses, and excludes self-employment income and overtime premiums; the annual salary is not an individual's actual-hours income, and the median is not starting pay.

Receive customer orders and repeat them back for confirmation → weigh and grind and extract according to recipes and standard procedures → prepare hot or cold beverages and complete serving → prepare or serve menu items and verify labels and shelf lives → deliver and explain to the customer → record orders and temperatures and exceptions and hand over the shift.

The 2022 catalog of national vocational skill standards promulgated by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security lists barista 4-03-02-08. This catalog confirms the name and code; the complete version of that standard was not obtained this time, and the catalog cannot be used to infer education, level conditions, or full equivalence with U.S. 35-3023.01. Precise occupational wages for China are still missing; the urban unit average for the accommodation and catering industry serves only as industry background.
Hygiene and safety and records

Employment and prospects (same-family parent occupation definition, not barista-only): the O*NET employment trends page states at the top “Employment data for Fast Food and Counter Workers,” and under that definition gives about 3,855,900 employed in 2025 and about 4,079,100 in 2035 (2025—2035 +6%, labeled faster than average (5% to 6%)), with about 827,400 job openings per year over the projection period (including growth and replacement). The corresponding chapter of the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook is the combined “Food and Beverage Serving and Related Workers” group: 5,143,000 employed in 2025, 2025—2035 +5% (faster than average), a change of +280,800, and about 1,078,500 annual openings (mostly from replacement needs). Both definitions are broader than barista-only, and the definition describes the occupational group and does not represent an individual hiring guarantee.

Confirm the condition of equipment and workstation → check freezer and refrigerator and heating equipment temperatures → clean and disinfect work areas and utensils and equipment according to procedure → verify food labels and shelf lives and arrange first-in-first-out → handle waste and keep the service area tidy → record temperatures and cleaning and exceptions.

The current O*NET industry page uses the parent occupation definition: accommodation and food services 87% and other industries (including retail) 13%, with no separate data year; sample job titles include Bobarista and Catering Barista. The O*NET hot technology page, based on January 1, 2025 to December 31 U.S. Lightcast job postings, lists Microsoft Office, Excel, and Word, each mentioned at below 1%; a posting mention is not an adoption rate, ability threshold, or uniform hiring condition.

Collaborate with baristas on the same shift and with back-of-house and front-desk colleagues; where hot beverages and steam and equipment operation, food allergens and temperature control, abnormal equipment temperature and shutdown, and refund, complimentary-item, and complaint handling authority are involved, act in accordance with the applicable jurisdiction and the competent authority and employer systems, do not decide on your own, and stop and report when equipment temperature is abnormal, food contamination is suspected, or the situation exceeds your authorization.

Baristas focus on beverage preparation and serving and counter service; food counter workers (the same-family parent occupation 35-3023.00) focus on a broader fast food and counter work scope, and the sub-identity on this page is barista; waiters and waitresses focus on tableside service of taking orders, serving, and settling bills; bartenders focus on mixing alcoholic beverages and compliance with alcohol regulations; cashiers focus on cashiering and settlement and accounts; food preparation workers focus on prep work and initial processing and assembling meals; hosts and hostesses focus on greeting and guiding and taking reservations. Adjacent occupations share store service, hygiene, and customer basics, but their work objects, deliverables, and authorization requirements differ, and positions involving alcohol and food safety are also subject to the licensing requirements of their respective jurisdictions.
Reviewable order, temperature, and cleaning records

Complete beverage preparation and serving and cleaning according to recipes and standard procedures, and leave a record explaining orders and output, equipment temperature checks and cleaning and disinfection handling, food label and shelf life verification, and customer feedback, exceptions, and the parts that remain uncertain, so that colleagues on the same shift and supervisors can review it on that basis.
Order, temperature, and cleaning records

The objects are coffee beans and tea leaves and dairy products and syrups and ingredients and prepared foods, utensils such as espresso machines and grinders and cold beverage equipment and freezers and refrigerators and heating equipment, and the cash register and ordering system; the basis is the customer's explicit requirements, recipe and standard procedure cards, the employer's and venue's food safety and hygiene procedures, and equipment and work safety rules.

Baristas (U.S. side O*NET 35-3023.01, Baristas) prepare or serve specialty coffee and other beverages and serve food such as baked goods and sandwiches to customers. The original official duty text is “Prepare or serve specialty coffee or other beverages. Serve food such as baked goods or sandwiches to patrons.”; there are 19 O*NET official tasks (17 core and 2 supplemental); core tasks include cleaning or disinfecting work areas and utensils and equipment (importance 96), collecting and processing customer payments (95), preparing or serving hot or cold beverages such as coffee and espresso drinks and blended coffee and tea (95), taking orders and relaying them to other colleagues for preparation (93), cleaning service or seating areas (86), making or serving menu items such as sandwiches or salads (86), wrapping and labeling or dating food for sale (84), checking freezer and refrigerator or heating equipment temperatures to ensure proper operation (83), taking out trash (82), describing menu items to customers or recommending products (81), demonstrating the use of retail equipment such as espresso machines (80), ordering and receiving or inventory replenishment or retail products (80), serving prepared foods such as muffins, biscotti, and bagels (77), restocking paper goods or beverage preparation materials at the customer service counter (77), providing product details such as coffee blends or brewing methods (73), setting up or restocking merchandise displays (73), and weighing and grinding and packaging coffee beans for customers (71); supplemental tasks include making signs labeling store products or events (46) and slicing fruit and vegetables and desserts or meats (35). This occupation is Job Zone 1–2 in the United States (SVP below 6.0) and is marked by O*NET as Bright Outlook; its wage, employment, and industry data are labeled on the O*NET page as taken from the same-family parent occupation 35-3023.00. This page does not constitute recipes, extraction parameters, or equipment operating instructions.
Order taking—preparation—serving—cleaning—records

Confirm the order and customer requirements → verify equipment temperature and materials and utensil condition → prepare beverages and serve according to recipes and verify labels and shelf lives → deliver and respond to customer feedback → clean and disinfect utensils and workstation → record orders and temperatures and exceptions according to procedure.
Reviewable order, temperature, and cleaning records

Order and output content, equipment temperature checks, utensil cleaning and disinfection and contaminated item handling, food label and shelf life verification, customer feedback and exceptions, and the parts that remain uncertain.
Self, colleagues on the same shift, and supervisors

Conclusions on beverage preparation and serving are borne by you according to your job duties; where abnormal equipment temperature and shutdown, food allergens and temperature control, suspected food contamination and recalls, and refund, complimentary-item, and complaint handling determinations are involved, they are made by personnel with the corresponding duties and authorization in accordance with the applicable jurisdiction and the competent authority and employer systems, and when an abnormality is found or the situation exceeds your authorization you must stop and report.
Education and preparation

O*NET lists 35-3023.01 (Baristas) as Job Zone 1–2 (SVP below 6.0); among the educational attainment the page publishes, 64% require less than a high school diploma, 29% require a high school diploma or equivalent, and 2% require a postsecondary certificate, and it notes that jobs in this zone usually require a high school diploma or equivalent, with experience requirements ranging from little to a few months to a year and on-the-job training ranging from a few days to a year. The corresponding chapter of the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook lists the typical entry-level education for this combined group as no formal educational credential, with no related work experience required and short-term on-the-job training, and notes that schedules often include early mornings and late nights and weekends and holidays, and that part-time work is common. The O*NET training page shows that no training programs for this occupation are registered nationwide, and the occupation summary also provides an Apprenticeship.gov apprenticeship opportunities entry point (searched by this occupational code); the certification page lists 3 national certifications (including coffee and food service fields). In mainland China, the barista 4-03-02-08 standard catalog has been verified; specific in-store mentoring must be verified with the employer. Article 44 of China's Food Safety Law requires food production and operation enterprises to carry out food safety knowledge training; Article 45 requires personnel engaged in work that comes into contact with directly edible food to undergo an annual health examination and obtain a health certificate before starting work. Specific equipment, refund, and management authority must be verified separately with the employer and cannot be inferred from education or occupational certificates.
Do not substitute for one another

Education, occupational training, industry certification, employer hiring, and in-store task authorization are different statuses: education and completion of training do not confer equipment operation or food safety determinations or shutdown and refund authority; each must be verified item by item according to employer and position and jurisdiction; this occupation is a sub-identity under 35-3023.00 (Fast Food and Counter Workers), and its wage and employment data are labeled on the source page as under the same-family parent occupation definition and cannot be used as barista-only data.

Verify at least six items before starting: the occupational definition and employer entity (O*NET 35-3023.01 is the U.S. definition, and wages and employment are under the same-family parent occupation 35-3023.00 definition); education and training; industry certifications (such as Certified Coffee Specialist); the scope of employer hiring and in-store authorization (including whether it covers equipment start-stop and refunds and complimentary items); food safety and equipment and venue hygiene requirements; and the employment arrangement and compensation basis (hourly wage and shifts and tips and part-time work).
Occupational definition

The U.S. identity and tasks are 35-3023.01, and the wage, employment, and industry pages explicitly adopt the parent occupation 35-3023.00. The employment table for the OOH Food and Beverage Serving and Related Workers chapter covers four groups — fast food and counter workers, nonrestaurant food servers, restaurant assistants, and hosts and hostesses — and does not include waiters and waitresses or bartenders; its combined group is not a barista subcategory. The 2022 catalog of national vocational skill standards promulgated by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security lists barista 4-03-02-08. This catalog confirms the name and code; the complete version of that standard was not obtained this time, and the catalog cannot be used to infer education, level conditions, or full equivalence with U.S. 35-3023.01. Precise national barista wages are still insufficient.
Education and preparation pathway

On the U.S. side, the O*NET educational composition is less than a high school diploma 64%, high school diploma or equivalent 29%, and postsecondary certificate 2%; the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook lists the typical entry-level education for this combined group as no formal educational credential and notes that skills are learned on the job; no training programs for this occupation are registered nationwide in O*NET, and there is also an apprenticeship opportunities entry point and 3 national certifications. In mainland China, the barista 4-03-02-08 standard catalog has been verified; specific education, experience, and mentoring must be verified separately with the employer. Article 44 of China's Food Safety Law requires food production and operation enterprises to carry out food safety knowledge training; Article 45 requires personnel engaged in work that comes into contact with directly edible food to undergo an annual health examination and obtain a health certificate before starting work. Specific equipment, refund, and management authority must be verified separately with the employer and cannot be inferred from education or occupational certificates.
Work and task authorization

Beverage preparation and serving and utensil disinfection must be carried out according to the employer's recipes and standard procedures and food safety procedures; where equipment start-stop and abnormal temperature handling, food allergens and temperature control, and refund, complimentary-item, and complaint handling are involved, this must be done according to employer procedures and authorization. On the U.S. side, O*NET lists 3 national certifications (which do not equal a hiring threshold or employer appointment); the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook notes that this combined group usually has no formal education or experience requirement and that skills are learned on the job. Verify the pre-job training and authorization process before starting, and do not infer it directly from education or experience.
Venue hygiene and equipment and food safety

The work environment and utensils and food must meet applicable hygiene and safety requirements (utensil cleaning and disinfection, food labels and shelf lives and temperature control, handling contaminated items and waste, cleaning workstations and floors, hot beverage and steam and equipment burn protection, and protection against prolonged standing and repetitive motions). O*NET work context shows 94% continuously or almost continuously stand, 67% continuously or almost continuously use hands to handle or feel objects and tools, 47% continuously or almost continuously make repetitive motions, 36% continuously or almost continuously walk or run, 86% have face-to-face discussions every day, 100% are in contact with others continuously, 66% work very close (within touching distance) to others, 43% are exposed to extreme heat or cold every day, 44% are exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise every day, 26% are exposed to minor burns, cuts, bites, or stings every day, 19% are exposed to contaminants every day, and 17% wear common protective or safety equipment every day; this page does not constitute recipes, extraction parameters, or equipment operating instructions.
Shifts and working hours

Work context shows 88% have a typical workweek of less than 40 hours, 52% have a regular schedule, and 40% an irregular schedule; 16% face time pressure every day (64% never); 23% deal with unpleasant or angry people every day (53% at least once a week); 24% are in conflict situations at least once a week. The BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook notes that this combined group's schedules often include early mornings and late nights and weekends and holidays, and that part-time work is common. When comparing positions, write the employment arrangement, shifts, tips, and overtime rules into the written terms.
Continuing training and review

The O*NET hot technology page, based on January 1, 2025 to December 31 U.S. Lightcast job postings, lists Microsoft Office, Excel, and Word, each mentioned at below 1%; a posting mention is not an adoption rate, ability threshold, or uniform hiring condition. Basic skills: active listening 60, speaking 56, monitoring 50, reading comprehension 47; knowledge: customer and personal service 89, administration and management 65, sales and marketing 62, food production 54, English language 52. Editorial suggestion: verify training, equipment authority, and review arrangements before starting.

All six directions share a background of store service, customer communication, and hygiene basics, but their work objects, deliverable results, and licensing and authorization requirements differ; the same store reception or serving experience cannot be directly converted into a license or task authorization for another direction (for example, bartending involves alcohol licensing), and this page only compares differences in duties under public definitions.

The basis for comparison is the official occupational description of O*NET 35-3023.01 and the related occupations list on the O*NET page (including the same-family parent occupation 35-3023.00), as well as the adjacent occupation relationships indicated in the routing materials; an adjacent relationship only describes proximity of duties and does not mean that licenses, authorizations, or positions are interchangeable.

The table below compares baristas with five adjacent directions along the same set of dimensions: occupational direction, core work and output, key differences, and which option better suits each preference.

Food counter workers (the same-family parent occupation 35-3023.00) cover a broader fast food and counter work scope; baristas are a sub-identity within them, specializing mainly in preparing and serving specialty coffee and other beverages.
If you prefer a broader scope of order taking and counter and serving work, compare food counter workers first; if you prefer specializing in beverage preparation and serving, baristas are suitable.
Complete order taking and serving and cleaning according to store standards, with output mainly orders and serving and store records.
Baristas and food counter workers

Waiters and waitresses focus on tableside service of taking orders, serving, and settling bills, usually involving serving order and tips; baristas focus on fast-paced counter beverage preparation and serving.
If you prefer tableside service and serving, compare waiters and waitresses first; if you prefer counter beverage preparation, baristas are suitable.
Complete order taking and serving and settlement in a restaurant, with output mainly tableside service and settlement records.
Baristas and waiters and waitresses

Bartenders focus on mixing alcoholic beverages and compliance with alcohol regulations and are usually subject to alcohol licensing and age verification requirements; baristas focus on nonalcoholic beverages and coffee and food and usually do not involve alcohol licensing.
If you prefer mixing alcoholic beverages, compare bartenders first; if you prefer coffee and nonalcoholic beverages, baristas are suitable.
Mix alcoholic beverages according to recipes and verify age and licensing requirements, with output mainly drink-list output and compliance records.
Baristas and bartenders

Cashiers focus on cashiering and settlement and accounts and making change and reconciliation and usually do not prepare beverages; baristas handle beverage preparation and serving and cashiering at the same time.
If you prefer cashiering and accounts, compare cashiers first; if you prefer doing both preparation and cashiering, baristas are suitable.
Complete cashiering and settlement and reconciliation, with output mainly transaction and reconciliation records.
Baristas and cashiers

Food preparation workers focus on prep work and initial processing and assembling meals and usually do not serve customers directly; baristas complete the full counter loop of preparation and serving and cashiering directly with customers.
If you prefer prep work and initial processing, compare food preparation workers first; if you prefer serving customers directly, baristas are suitable.
Complete prep work and initial processing and meal assembly, with output mainly prep and meal assembly records.
Baristas and food preparation workers

Hosts and hostesses focus on greeting and guiding and reservations and waiting-list management and usually do not prepare or cashier; baristas focus on preparation and serving and cashiering, with reception only one part of the job.
If you prefer reception and reservation management, compare hosts and hostesses first; if you prefer preparation and serving, baristas are suitable.
Complete greeting and guiding and reservations and waiting-list arrangements, with output mainly reception and seating records.
Baristas and hosts and hostesses

Conclusion: the basis for choosing a direction is the work object, deliverable results, and licensing requirements, not whether both work in food and beverage outlets; after choosing a direction, verify item by item the training, licensing, and task authorization requirements of the target direction.

First practice the order-taking—preparation—serving—cleaning—recording loop to fluency on fixed fictional materials: given a fictional menu and recipe card, a fictional equipment temperature check sheet, and a fictional order and cleaning record sheet, write out in order orders and output, temperature checks and cleaning and disinfection handling, food label and shelf life verification, and how to write exceptions and open items, and only then talk about positions; at the same time verify the target employer's pre-job training and in-store task authorization requirements.
Practicing baristas

Use order taking and order relaying, inventory and supply ordering summaries, scheduling and peak forecasting references, and preliminary classification of equipment prompts and alarms to improve efficiency, but recipe and extraction and output quality determinations, judgment and handling of abnormal equipment temperature, food allergens and temperature control, and refund, complimentary-item, and complaint handling are still borne by you and authorized personnel in accordance with the applicable jurisdiction and employer systems, and system output must go through on-site verification and human review before entering formal records.
Chain brand stores and independent coffee shops and retail, hotel, and institutional beverage bars

When introducing ordering, inventory, or scheduling systems, specify which steps may use them, the rules for protecting customer information and payment information, and the responsible persons for review and authorization when abnormal equipment temperature and food safety and refunds and complimentary items are involved, retaining the final judgment and handling decisions of responsible personnel.
Training institutions and mentors

Focus teaching on recipes and standard procedures and output consistency, equipment operation and temperature checks and cleaning, utensil cleaning and disinfection, food labels and shelf lives and allergen control, and customer communication and complaint handling, while training critical use of system prompts and search results, avoiding substituting tool suggestions for on-site observation and human review.

Editorial suggestion: assistance uses such as order text, inventory summaries, menu descriptions, and record drafts can be evaluated, testing accuracy, data permissions, and human review first. Insufficient evidence: the sources reviewed this time do not give a barista AI adoption rate, productivity, or replacement result. Beverage preparation, abnormal temperature, and allergen handling still follow on-site procedures.

Direct answer: the main risks include hot beverage and steam and equipment burns, food allergens and temperature control, customer information and payment information leaks, repetitive motion and prolonged standing injuries, out-of-control temperature and cleaning and batch records, and unclear food safety and shutdown and refund authority; the control method is to act according to recipes and the applicable jurisdiction and the competent authority and employer procedures, and to stop and report when an abnormality appears.

subject.name: Baristas
subject.summary: Baristas prepare and serve specialty coffee and other beverages and serve food such as baked goods and sandwiches to customers: taking orders and relaying them, preparing and serving hot and cold beverages according to recipes, weighing and grinding and packaging coffee beans, preparing and serving menu items, wrapping and labeling and dating, checking equipment temperatures, cleaning and disinfecting work areas and utensils and equipment, cleaning service and seating areas, ordering and restocking and arranging displays, describing the menu and demonstrating equipment use, and collecting and processing payments. The U.S. side corresponds to O*NET 35-3023.01 (Baristas), which is Job Zone 1–2 (SVP below 6.0) and is marked by O*NET as Bright Outlook; its wage, employment, and industry data are explicitly labeled on the O*NET page as taken from the same-family parent occupation 35-3023.00 (Fast Food and Counter Workers), and the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook chapter is also the combined “Food and Beverage Serving and Related Workers” group, neither of which is equivalent to a barista-only definition. On the mainland China side, this page has not obtained a precise national occupational wage distribution for baristas, so the boundary of no data that can be safely used is retained; industry wage statistics cannot provide a national occupational median or a uniform starting wage, and the Chinese page language is not treated as a China equivalent occupation or wage mapping.
